title: Fluorescence detection methods for microfluidic droplet platforms
protocol: Spin coat SU8-50 on a Si wafer at 3000 rpm for 30 seconds.
Soft bake the wafer on a hot-plate at 65°C for 5 minutes.
Continue soft baking at 95°C for 30 minutes to densify the film.
Expose the SU8 resist with 360-440 nm radiation at 300 mJ/2 under the appropriate mask.
Bake the wafer at 65°C for 2 minutes after exposure.
Further bake the wafer at 95°C for 4 minutes.
Develop the unexposed areas with Micrpoposit EC solvent, stirring, for 5 minutes.
Rinse the wafer with fresh EC solvent and dry it under gas to generate a clean surface.
Treat the wafer with hexane washes.
Proceed with methanol washes on the wafer.
Evaporate trichloro(1,1,2,2-perfluorocyclohexyl)silane onto the surface in a desiccator for 40 minutes.
Mix Sylgard 184 in a 10:1 ratio of resin to crosslinker.
Pour the mixed Sylgard over the master.
Degas the mixture in a desiccator.
Cure the device for one hour at 65°C.
Cut and peel the cured PDMS from the master.
Create access holes using a biopsy punch.
Spread 8 g of the resin evenly in a Petri dish.
Cure another layer of PDMS for 20 minutes at 65°C.
Place the prepared top layer on the bottom layer.
Cure overnight at 65°C.
Peel the chips from the Petri dish and dice for use.
Fill syringes with the required solutions, ensuring no air bubbles remain.
Mix oil and surfactant to form the continuous phase for droplet generation.
Fit tubing of the same internal diameter as the syringe needle tips onto one end of the needles.
Cut the tubing to the shortest possible length.
Connect the other ends of the tubing directly to the holes punched in the PDMS substrate.
Connect the outlet port of the chip to tubing and direct it into a collector.
Mount the syringes on a syringe pump.
Define the desired infusing flow-rate for each phase.
Flush the oil phase alone through any microfluidic channels before introducing the aqueous phase.
Use a confocal microscope with automated submicron positioning capacity.
Select water-soluble fluorescent molecules with high quantum yields.
Excite the molecules using a laser matching the absorption of the fluorophore.
For FITC and Alexa-Fluor 488, use a 488 nm diode laser.
For Texas Red or APC, excite using a 633 nm He/Ne laser.
Use pulsed lasers with repetition rates of several MHz for FLIM experiments.
Control beam height and direction with beam-steering mirrors and optics.
Reflect the laser beam into the objective lens using a dichroic mirror.
Install a dual-band dichroic mirror if two lasers are used simultaneously.
Use an infinity-corrected, high numerical aperture (NA) microscope objective.
Select the objective appropriately for tall microchannels (>100 μm).
Collect fluorescence emitted by the sample using the same high NA objective.
Remove any residual excitation light using a single or dual-band emission filter.
Focus the fluorescence emission onto a 75 μm pinhole using a plano-convex lens.
Position the pinhole in the confocal plane of the microscope objective.
Split the fluorescent signal onto two detectors using another dichroic mirror.
Filter fluorescence reflected by the dichroic mirror with an hq540/80 m filter.
Focus filtered fluorescence onto the first ('green') detector using a plano-convex lens.
For experiments involving a secondary red fluorophore, filter fluorescence transmitted by the dichroic mirror with an hq640lp filter.
Focus filtered fluorescence onto the second ('red') detector using another plano-convex lens.
Use avalanche photodiodes for detection of fluorescence photons.
Mix reagents off-chip to achieve the desired mixture and concentration.
Alternatively, bring reagents separately into the chip for combination prior to droplet formation.
Stir cell suspension in the syringe to prevent cell condensation over the course of the experiment.
Couple the electronic signal from the avalanche photodiode detector to a multifunction DAQ device for data logging.
Connect the detectors to a Time-Correlated Single Photon Counting (TCSPC) card for FLIM experiments.
Obtain fluorescence lifetime data using TCSPC methodology.
Fit each detected fluorescent photon to an incident laser pulse.
Assign a delay time to each emitted fluorescent photon.
Deconvolute raw data with the instrument response function (IRF).
Use a low concentration Auramine-O solution to obtain IRF.
Culture Escherichia coli Top 10 strain in Luria-Bertani broth overnight.
Match the optical density of the cell culture to 0.5 prior to experiments.
Use 0.4 μM SYTO9 and 1 μM propidium iodide for detecting cell viability.
Focus the optical probe volume at half the height of a microchannel along which droplets are flowing.
Form droplets from two aqueous solutions, each containing a fluorophore with different characteristic fluorescent lifetimes.
Carry out experiments along the entire width of the channel at 1 μm intervals starting from one side.
Differentiate signal bursts (associated with droplets) from the noise background of the oil phase using an algorithm.
Establish the duration of each burst.
Implement a second algorithm to extract delay time and intensity values along the length of each droplet.
Use a Maximum Likelihood Estimator (MLE) algorithm to evaluate the fluorescence lifetime for each droplet in the experiment.
Average the lifetime values for all the droplets in the experiment to reduce the final error of the MLE calculation.
Obtain a lifetime trajectory for each width.
Combine all the trajectories in a 2D map.
Reinterpret raw experimental data files into an appropriate computing language for further analysis.
Write specific codes to access data contained in files from complex experiments such as those for FLIM.
Since the probe volume is fixed and droplets are flowing across that position, obtain a trajectory of lifetime values along the length of the droplets at that particular width.
Average the lifetime trajectory among 6000 droplets for a characteristic profile.
Combine trajectories throughout the entire width of the channel to form a 2D concentration map.
Reduce the standard error of results by averaging among a large number of droplets (1% of standard error with a 95% confidence interval).
Assume that all droplets are practically identical for the determination method of lifetime trajectory.
Confirm the reproducibility of results regardless of individual droplets analyzed or the amount of droplets used in calculations.
